title: Mata v. Avianca, Inc. — Opinion and Order on Sanctions
author: Judge P. Kevin Castel

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Filing duties: AI use never displaces inquiry
st.an: Mata supports the cluster’s central proposition that existing duties of reasonable inquiry and candour continue to govern filings, while ordinary legal error is not automatically sanctionable. It also directly supports the cluster’s qualified account of sanctions: in its Second Circuit context, court-initiated Rule 11 sanctions require subjective bad faith, and sanctions should be restrained and deterrence-focused.

When, as here, a court considers whether to impose sanctions sua sponte,  it “is akin to the court’s inherent power of contempt,” and, “like contempt, sua sponte sanctions  in those circumstances should issue only upon a finding of subjective bad faith.”  Muhammad,  732 F.3d at 108.

st.t: Litigation responsibility: Sanctions follow conduct and authority
st.an: Mata directly supports the cluster’s central proposition that AI assistance is permissible but attorneys remain accountable for filing accuracy. It also supports the importance of post-discovery conduct by faulting counsel for continuing to defend fabricated authorities after judicial warnings.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s human-led, verification-centred model: AI assistance is permissible, but lawyers retain responsibility for checking filings. It provides case-specific evidence that failed verification and continued reliance on fabricated authorities can trigger sanctions under existing rules; it does not establish general model error rates or broader productivity effects.
qs: Technological advances are commonplace and there is  nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance.
But  existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings.

kp.k: AI assistance does not displace attorneys’ gatekeeping responsibilities
kp.d: Judge Castel distinguishes permissible assistance from reliable AI tools from attorneys’ continuing responsibility under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11 to ensure filing accuracy. The decision sanctions the lawyers’ conduct, not AI use as such.
qs: Technological advances are commonplace and there is nothing inherently improper about using a reliable artificial intelligence tool for assistance.
But existing rules impose a gatekeeping role on attorneys to ensure the accuracy of their filings.

kp.k: ChatGPT generated nonexistent authorities subsequently submitted to court
kp.d: The court found that Schwartz researched and drafted the March 1, 2023 opposition using ChatGPT, while LoDuca signed and filed it. Respondents ultimately acknowledged that six purported decisions were generated by ChatGPT and did not exist. The findings document fabricated citations, quotations, judicial authorship and facts, alongside genuine authorities misrepresented as supporting the arguments. This is evidence of a specific sanctions incident, not a measurement of model error rates.
qs: Respondents have now acknowledged that the “Varghese”, “Miller”, “Petersen”, “Shaboon”, “Martinez” and “Durden” decisions were generated by ChatGPT and do not exist.
At the time that he prepared the Affirmation in Opposition, Mr. Schwartz did not have the full text of any “decision” generated by ChatGPT.

kp.k: Limited research access preceded reliance on an unfamiliar chatbot
kp.d: Schwartz attributed his turn to ChatGPT to the firm’s limited federal-case access through Fastcase and lack of Westlaw or LexisNexis accounts. He had not previously used ChatGPT and mistakenly treated it as a search engine. The court found his description of AI as merely supplementing research misleading: it supplied his substantive arguments after the initial unsuccessful Fastcase search.
qs: It uses a legal research service called Fastcase and does not maintain Westlaw or LexisNexis accounts.
When Mr. Schwartz began to research the Montreal Convention, the firm’s Fastcase account had limited access to federal cases.
He cited and quoted only from excerpts generated by the chatbot.

kp.k: Requests for supporting precedents elicited fabricated legal support
kp.d: The recorded prompts began with an instruction to argue that bankruptcy tolled the Montreal Convention limitations period, then sought specific supporting holdings and additional cases. The court found that ChatGPT supplied fabricated authorities in response. Later screenshots also showed the chatbot assuring Schwartz that its authorities were real and available through established legal sources; the court rejected his shifting explanations about when and how those assurances affected his beliefs.
qs: When directed to “provide case law”, “show me specific holdings”, “show me more cases” and “give me some cases”, the chatbot complied by making them up.
ChatGPT responded that it had supplied “real” authorities that could be found through Westlaw, LexisNexis and the Federal Reporter.

kp.k: Delegating research did not excuse the signing attorney
kp.d: LoDuca relied on a colleague of more than twenty-five years, reviewed the opposition for style rather than legal accuracy, and made no inquiry into the research. The court separately assessed his conduct and found subjective bad faith in signing without inquiry, particularly given his knowledge of Schwartz’s unfamiliarity with the relevant federal law and the firm’s research limitations. It also found he swore to the later affidavit without a basis for its assertions.
qs: Before executing the Affirmation, Mr. LoDuca did not review any judicial authorities cited in his affirmation.
But signing and filing that affirmation after making no “inquiry” was an act of subjective bad faith.
While an inadequate inquiry may not suggest bad faith, the absence of any inquiry supports a finding of bad faith.

kp.k: Continuing advocacy after warnings compounded the original failures
kp.d: Avianca’s March 15 brief questioned the authorities’ existence, and the court’s April 11 and 12 orders required their production. Respondents nevertheless submitted purported excerpts on April 25 and first acknowledged the fabrications on May 25. The court explains that Rule 11 obligations extend to later advocacy and failure to correct a pending submission, rather than ending when it is filed.
qs: An attorney’s compliance with Rule 11(b)(2) is not assessed solely at the moment that the paper is submitted.
The failure to correct a prior statement in a pending motion is the later advocacy of that statement and is subject to sanctions.
At no time has any Respondent written to this Court seeking to withdraw the March 1 Affirmation in Opposition or advise the Court that it may no longer rely upon it.

kp.k: Sanctions rested on subjective bad faith, not merely mistakes
kp.d: For these court-initiated sanctions, the court applied a subjective-bad-faith standard, distinguishing conscious avoidance from negligent or sloppy research. Findings included Schwartz’s failure to disclose unsuccessful searches and his misleading accounts of AI reliance, alongside LoDuca’s knowing falsehood about vacation to obtain an extension. Each lawyer’s knowledge and conduct were assessed separately.
qs: Poor and sloppy research would merely have been objectively unreasonable.
But Mr. Schwartz was aware of facts that alerted him to the high probability that “Varghese” and “Zicherman” did not exist and consciously avoided confirming that fact.

These shifting and contradictory explanations, submitted even after the Court raised the possibility of Rule 11 sanctions, undermine the credibility of Mr. Schwartz and support a finding of subjective bad faith.

kp.k: Fabricated opinions harm clients, courts and public trust
kp.d: The court identifies wasted adversary resources and judicial time, possible loss of authentic arguments for the client, reputational harm to falsely named judges and parties, and cynicism about the profession and judicial system. These are the court’s account of harms and potential consequences, not quantified findings about market-wide costs.
qs: The opposing party wastes time and money in exposing the deception.
The client may be deprived of arguments based on authentic judicial precedents.
It promotes cynicism about the legal profession and the American judicial system.

kp.k: Existing sanctions powers covered fabricated AI-generated legal authorities
kp.d: The court held that fake opinions cannot support arguments under Rule 11(b)(2), sanctioned respondents under Rule 11 and alternatively its inherent authority, and held the firm jointly and severally liable because no exceptional circumstances justified exemption. It found no violation of 18 U.S.C. § 505 because the fake opinions bore no signature or seal, and declined separate sanctions under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 because dilatory tactics and delay were not among the harms.
qs: An attempt to persuade a court or oppose an adversary by relying on fake opinions is an abuse of the adversary system.
The Levidow Firm is jointly and severally liable for the Rule 11(b)(2) violations of Mr. LoDuca and Mr. Schwartz.
Each of the Respondents is sanctioned under Rule 11 and, alternatively, under the inherent power of this Court.

kp.k: Remedies combined monetary deterrence, notification and acknowledged remediation
kp.d: The June 22, 2023 order imposed a single $5,000 penalty jointly and severally, payable to the court within 14 days, and required notification with supporting documents to Mata and the judges falsely identified as opinion authors. The court credited remorse, publicity, absence of disciplinary history and low likelihood of repetition. It considered additional education redundant given the firm’s arranged technological-competence and AI training and intended notarization training; opposing counsel had not sought fees, and no compelled apology was ordered.
qs: A penalty of $5,000 is jointly and severally imposed on Respondents and shall be paid into the Registry of this Court within 14 days of this Opinion and Order.
The Levidow Firm has arranged for outside counsel to conduct a mandatory Continuing Legal Education program on technological competence and artificial intelligence programs.
The Court will not require an apology from Respondents because a compelled apology is not a sincere apology.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Judge Castel permits reliable AI assistance in principle but holds that attorneys retain responsibility for checking filings; this case demonstrates fabricated authorities entering litigation through ChatGPT.
pts.d: In this sanctions opinion, Castel treats AI as a possible research and drafting aid, not a replacement for attorneys’ gatekeeping obligations under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11. He finds that ChatGPT generated nonexistent cases and that the respondents submitted and continued advocating those authorities. The opinion does not predict productivity gains, job displacement or legal-market restructuring. Its concrete implications concern verification, candour and accountability when AI is used in legal work.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence is a judicially examined sanctions incident, supported by filings, testimony, chatbot exchanges and checks of purported authorities—not a measured model error rate.
pts.d: Castel’s findings draw on the June 8, 2023 hearing, sworn declarations, the submitted research history, the court’s searches, docket and reporter comparisons, and confirmation from the Eleventh Circuit clerk that a purported opinion was not authentic. Respondents acknowledged six named decisions were generated by ChatGPT and did not exist. Schwartz testified that he had mistaken ChatGPT for a search engine and relied on it for his substantive arguments; the court rejected aspects of his explanations and found conscious avoidance and misleading statements. Rule 11 and cited precedents supply the legal authority for continued attorney responsibility. This single case establishes the conduct examined here, not a general frequency of AI fabrication.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The conclusions concern conduct in March–June 2023 and turn on unreliable submissions, continued advocacy after warnings, and subjective bad faith—not AI use alone.
pts.d: The initial submission was filed March 1, 2023; the adversary questioned the authorities on March 15; the court ordered production on April 11 and 12; respondents supplied purported opinions on April 25 and first acknowledged ChatGPT-generated fabrications on May 25. The sanctions order issued June 22. Castel expressly distinguishes reliable AI assistance from misconduct and says prompt candour would have materially changed the record. In this court-initiated sanctions proceeding, he applied a subjective-bad-faith standard and distinguished conscious avoidance from merely poor research. The obligation to correct unsupported contentions continues after filing. The opinion specifies no future horizon for changes in AI capability.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Unchecked fabricated authorities expose lawyers and firms to sanctions and impose costs or risks on opponents, clients, judges and public confidence.
pts.d: Castel identifies wasted opposing-party resources and diverted court time, possible loss of authentic arguments for clients, reputational harm to judges and parties falsely implicated, and cynicism about the profession and judicial system. These are the court’s stated harms and potential harms, not quantified estimates. In this case, two lawyers and their primarily New York state-court practice were jointly and severally assessed a single $5,000 penalty and required to notify the client and judges falsely identified as authors. The firm reported an expanded research subscription and technological-competence training. These consequences illustrate verification and institutional accountability rather than a general claim about employment or pricing.
